sections.heading: C — Guide signs and pavement markings
sections.markdown:
## C — Guide signs and pavement markings

FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A01
Electronic flashing arrow panels warn approaching drivers of lane closures and direct a move or merge left or right. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A01
Begin the required merge well before reaching an electronic arrow panel. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A01
An electronic panel showing caution rather than a directional arrow warns of a work area beside the travel lane. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A01
Work-zone barrels, tubes, cones and vertical panels guide traffic through changed patterns and away from road-work hazards. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A01
Guide signs identify intersecting roads, destinations, attractions and services such as hospitals, fuel, food and lodging. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A01
Guide signs are usually horizontal rectangles. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A01
Highway and expressway guide signs use white lettering against green. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A01
A typical highway exit is signed twice in advance and again at the exit. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A01
Repeated highway signs help drivers notice an exit in fast or heavy traffic and allow time for needed lane changes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A01
Exit numbers correspond to mile markers and can be used to estimate the distance between exits. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A01
In the handbook's mileage example, Exit 95 and Exit 20 are 75 miles apart. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A01
An EXIT ONLY panel means its lane leaves the highway as a ramp instead of continuing through the interchange. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A01
A driver in an EXIT ONLY lane may change lanes, but must leave the highway if remaining in that lane. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A02
An exit-number panel at the left of a green guide sign indicates a left-side highway exit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A02
An exit-number panel at the right of a green guide sign indicates a right-side highway exit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A02
When a guide sign includes white arrows, those arrows point toward the exit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A02
The red, white and blue shield identifies an interstate highway. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A02
Even-numbered interstates with one or two digits generally run east and west. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A02
Odd-numbered interstates with one or two digits generally run north and south. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A02
For east-west interstate numbering, the national pattern increases from I-10 in the south toward I-94 in the north. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A02
For north-south interstate numbering, the pattern increases from I-5 in the west toward I-95 in the east. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A02
The handbook places I-76 in southern Pennsylvania and I-84 and I-80 in northern Pennsylvania. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A02
The handbook places I-79 in western Pennsylvania and I-95 in eastern Pennsylvania. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A02
Interstates with three-digit numbers connect to other major highways. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A02
A three-digit interstate whose first digit is even usually connects with interstates at both ends and may form a loop or beltway. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A02
I-276 in Philadelphia is the handbook's example of a route with an even first digit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A02
A three-digit interstate whose first digit is odd is usually a spur connecting to an interstate at only one end. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F28 | anchor: A02
I-180 in Williamsport is the handbook's example of a spur that may lead into a city center. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F29 | anchor: A02
Mile markers measure from a route's entry into the state, or from its beginning when the route does not reach a state border. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F30 | anchor: A02
Mile-marker numbering starts from zero at the west for east-west roads and at the south for north-south roads. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F31 | anchor: A02
Mile-marker values rise when traveling east or north and fall when traveling west or south. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F32 | anchor: A02
In the handbook's I-80 example, entering Pennsylvania from the west encounters Mile 1 before higher markers farther east. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec06-F33 | anchor: A02
Reading mile markers helps locate the vehicle when requesting roadside assistance. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0024]

Misconceptions: an exit-only lane becomes a ramp; a broken line permits a crossing only where the stated safety conditions allow it; a shared center turn lane is not a passing lane.
Mnemonics: read the route, locate the exit, then check the line color and pattern.
Glossary: a trailblazer directs traffic toward a route; a spur usually connects at one end; a center turn lane serves left turns from opposing directions.
Dynamic facts: no officeholder, local answer or time-varying value is asserted; handbook edition currency is tracked as source debt in the authority part.

items.why: This is a distinct learnable group of handbook rules requiring its own recall and application practice.
